content: Labour is a natural physiological process, but it is often accompanied by significant pain and discomfort. Various methods are employed to alleviate this pain, including pharmacological approaches such as epidurals, opioids, and inhaled analgesia, as well as non-pharmacological techniques like hypnosis and acupuncture. Non-opioid drugs represent a pharmacological option for managing mild to moderate pain during labour. The objective of this review was to evaluate the evidence regarding the effectiveness and safety of non-opioid drugs in relieving labour pain. The search for relevant studies was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group’s Trials Register as of February 15, 2012. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared non-opioid drugs—such as non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), paracetamol, antispasmodics, sedatives, and antihistamines—with placebo, standard care, other non-opioid drugs, or opioids. Quasi-RCTs and cross-over trials were excluded, while cluster-randomized RCTs were eligible but none were identified. Two independent reviewers assessed the studies for inclusion, extracted data, and evaluated the risk of bias. Disagreements were resolved through discussion with a third reviewer, and the data were verified for accuracy. A total of 19 studies involving 2863 women were included in the review. These studies were divided into three main comparison groups: 15 studies compared non-opioid drugs with placebo or no treatment (2133 women), three studies compared non-opioid drugs with opioids (563 women), and three studies compared different types or doses of non-opioid drugs (590 women). Some studies included multiple groups and were therefore included in more than one comparison. The results showed minimal differences between groups for most comparisons. However, certain findings were notable. Sedatives were associated with better pain relief compared to placebo (mean difference (MD) -22.00; 95% confidence interval (CI) -35.86 to -8.14, based on one trial with 50 women). Sedatives and antihistamines also resulted in higher satisfaction with pain relief compared to placebo (risk ratio (RR) 1.59; 95% CI 1.15 to 2.21, based on two trials with 204 women; RR 1.80; 95% CI 1.16 to 2.79, based on one trial with 223 women). Additionally, sedatives improved satisfaction with the overall childbirth experience compared to placebo (RR 2.16; 95% CI 1.34 to 3.47, based on one trial with 40 women). When comparing non-opioid drugs to opioids, women who received NSAIDs or antihistamines were less likely to be satisfied with pain relief than those who received opioids (RR 0.50; 95% CI 0.27 to 0.94, based on one trial with 76 women; RR 0.73; 95% CI 0.54 to 0.98, based on one trial with 223 women). Among antihistamines, women who received hydroxyzine were more likely to report satisfaction with pain relief compared to those who received promethazine (RR 1.21; 95% CI 1.02 to 1.43, based on one trial with 289 women). Sedatives were also associated with greater satisfaction with pain relief compared to antihistamines (RR 1.52; 95% CI 1.06 to 2.17, based on one study with 157 women). It is important to note that the majority of the included studies were conducted over 30 years ago, and the risk of bias was unclear for most quality domains. Overall, opioids appeared to provide superior satisfaction with pain relief compared to non-opioids, while non-opioids were more effective than placebo in terms of pain relief and satisfaction with the childbirth experience. However, there was limited data and no significant evidence regarding the safety outcomes of non-opioid drugs. In conclusion, the findings of this review indicate insufficient evidence to support the use of non-opioid drugs alone for managing pain during labour.
